title: Linked Lists: Traversal
oneLiner: No indexes here -- walk node to node by following .Next until it's null.
keyTakeaway: Linked lists trade the array's O(1) random access for O(1) insert/delete at a known position -- the only way to reach position i is to walk i steps from the head.
explanation: A linked list stores each value in its own node, a small object holding the value and a reference (`Next`) to the next node; the first node is the head, and the last node's `Next` is null, meaning "no node". It has no index -- there's no nums[3]. The only way to get anywhere is to start at the head and follow each node's `Next` pointer until you hit null. This is the single most important habit to build before touching anything else with linked lists (reversal, cycle detection, merging): a `while (current != null) { ...; current = current.Next; }` loop. Watch out for the classic bug -- advancing the pointer before you've read/used the current node's value, which silently skips the head.

visualizationSteps.message: current = head. There's no index to jump around with -- the only way forward is current.Next.
Visit node 0 (val 4), record it, then move current = current.Next.
Visit node 1 (val 8), record it, then move current = current.Next.
Visit node 2 (val 15), record it, then move current = current.Next.
Visit node 3 (val 16), record it, then move current = current.Next.
Visit node 4 (val 23), record it, then move current = current.Next.
current.Next is null -- end of the list. Every node was visited exactly once, O(n).

complexity.note: Walking the list is O(n) time with O(1) pointers, but this version collects every value into an output array, which is O(n) space.

referenceSolutions.python:
def traverse_to_array(head):
    result = []
    node = head
    while node is not None:
        result.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    return result
